headline: No agreement on how to split FY2028 budget cuts between town and schools, or on using reserves.

decision_titles: Budgeting out-of-district special education costs from prior-year receipts
Split of FY2028 budget reductions and use of reserves
plain_text:
Sutton Leadership Working Group 
Virtual Meeting 
Tuesday, October 13, 2026 – 8:30 AM 
Meeting Minutes 
Members Present: Ken Stuart (Town Moderator), Christine Watkins (Select Board), Jesse 
Limanek (Select Board), George Watson (Finance & Warrant Advisory Committee), Timothy 
Harrison (Finance & Warrant Advisory Committee), Erin Reid-Eriksen (School Committee), 
Chris Matera (School Committee) 
Non-voting Members Present: Austin Cyganiewicz (Town Manager), Harrison McKinlay 
(School Business Manager), Caitlin Paget (Superintendent of Schools), Matt Belsito (Fire Chief), 
Thomas Calouro (Police Chief) 
Mr. Stuart called the meeting to order at 9:03 AM and conducted a roll call. 
1. Approval of Minutes 
On a motion by Mr. Limanek, seconded by Mr. Matera, the Group approved the September 15, 
2026 minutes by unanimous vote.  
2. Out-of-District Special Education Costs 
Ms. Paget and Mr. McKinlay described the budget pressure created by out-of-district 
placements, which are legally required and very challenging to forecast. Mr. McKinlay reviewed 
ten years of circuit breaker data: the state reimburses 75% of eligible costs above a per-student 
threshold (now above $53,000), one year in arrears, leaving roughly $1.3 million of FY2027 
tuition in the operating budget. The in-house special education transportation program brought 
in about $463,000 in revolving fund revenue last year; contracting the service is estimated at 
$1.0–$1.2 million. 
Mr. McKinlay cautioned that full state funding of circuit breaker could remove a check on tuition 
increases and might come at the expense of Chapter 70, and recommended continuing to 
budget from prior-year receipts. Ms. Watkins suggested legislative advocacy on the threshold. 
The Group also discussed school choice: choice-out charges are deducted from net state aid on 
the cherry sheet ($332,000 in FY2027, up from $115,000 five to six years ago), while school 
choice revenue has helped offset high school salaries and rebuild reserves. State data showed 
38 students choiced out and 45 choiced in. Ms. Reid-Eriksen noted that tuition and emergency 
repairs draw down funds available for general education, and Mr. Watson observed that any 
override should be paired with a fresh look at how the Town budgets. 
3. Facilities and the Proposed DPW Reorganization 
Mr. Matera asked whether town and school facility maintenance could be consolidated, through 
a single maintenance contract or a DPW facilities division. Mr. Cyganiewicz said several nearby 
communities operate this way, but savings have not been analyzed and any change would 
require bargaining on both sides and dedicated funding to be effective. 
Mr. Cyganiewicz then summarized his outreach to all municipal departments. Common themes 
were level staffing for many years, duties absorbed by existing staff, informal facilities 
management, and reactive capital planning. He presented a draft DPW reorganization for the
May Annual Town Meeting: the highway superintendent would become DPW director, with an 
operations manager, two mechanics, a facilities and grounds division, a transfer station 
supervisor, and an engineering division, growing the department from 15 positions to a draft 
total of 27 at an estimated cost of about $1 million. The plan would require impact bargaining 
with the affected unions. 
Requests and needs raised by departments included: four firefighters to expand day coverage 
and add weekends, with Chief Belsito confirming the call force remains necessary. Two patrol 
officers to raise shift minimums from two to three and a second lieutenant for state accreditation 
and compliance, per Chief Calouro. An assistant planner; added daytime inspection hours; 
$15,000 more for tax title legal costs; a senior center activities coordinator ($45,000–$55,000); 
part-time staffing and equipment funds for communications and cable; and an adult services 
librarian (about $50,000) plus $12,000 in materials to meet the 19% MBLC appropriation 
requirement. Mr. Cyganiewicz estimated recurring capital needs at $2.0–$2.5 million annually, 
noting that a new DPW facility would cost $20–$40 million, and cautioned that current revenues 
cannot support an added $2 million in FY2028 or FY2029. 
4. FY2028 Deficit and Budget Direction 
Mr. Cyganiewicz reported that the projected FY2028 deficit has grown from $1.66 million to $2.2 
million, driven by the increase in the school cap to 3.75% and an early estimate of a 15% health 
insurance increase, following increases of 19% and 11% in the prior two years. At a 2.5% levy 
increase and $250,000 in new growth, the deficit is projected at about $3.6 million in FY2029, 
$5.2 million in FY2030, and $11.2 to $11.3 million by FY2033. The upward revision to FY2027 
new growth is already reflected in the base. 
He relayed the Select Board’s direction to close the FY2028 gap with a strategic use of reserves 
and a reduction in budget requests across town and school. He noted this differs from the Tri-
Board’s September recommendation to bridge FY2028 with reserves alone and cautioned that 
heavy reliance on reserves runs against bond rating agency guidance. Mr. Harrison asked 
whether the OPEB trust could provide one-time relief. Mr. Cyganiewicz said it had not been 
considered and runs counter to best practice given the $25 million liability. Ms. Watkins 
suggested the Group consider pausing the additional contribution of roughly $350,000 made 
each fall. 
On the allocation of the reductions, Mr. Cyganiewicz had offered a 50/50 split ($550,000 each) 
for discussion; a Select Board member suggested roughly 65/35, based on the schools’ share of 
the budget. Mr. McKinlay objected that the schools have not received a proportional share of 
new growth and noted that further cuts would continue a downward trend in spending above the 
state net school spending requirement, which municipal health insurance and benefits have 
counted toward since 1993. Mr. Cyganiewicz said the right split falls between 50/50 and 70/30 
and that he needs direction. Mr. Matera floated 60/40. Using that figure as an illustration, Ms. 
Paget said a $660,000 school reduction would mean seven to nine full-time positions, mostly 
newer teachers by seniority, with cuts concentrated in electives and Advanced Placement and 
larger general education class sizes; special education services would be protected. Mr. 
Cyganiewicz said a $550,000 reduction from the $8.6 million municipal budget (excluding 
benefits) would likewise reduce services across departments. Ms. Watkins noted that school-
related costs, including roughly $3.1 million in health insurance carried on the municipal side, 
represent about $25 million of the $42 million budget, or about 60%. 
The Group did not reach consensus on the split of reductions or on the use of the reserve funds. 
Mr. Stuart noted that time was short and two School Committee members had left the meeting. 
Mr. Cyganiewicz asked members to bring specific proposals to the next meeting, as he hopes to 
issue budget instructions to departments soon. 
6. Next Meeting and Adjournment 
The next meeting was set for Tuesday, November 3, 2026 at 8:30 AM, with 90 minutes allotted. 
On a motion by Mr. Watson, seconded by Ms. Watkins, the Group voted to adjourn at 11:25 AM.
